The Saputo Toufexis team represents clients who are seeking the top attorneys in the field. Accordingly, our attorneys have made consistently outstanding legal representation the hallmark of our boutique criminal defense practice.

We’re not just DWI lawyers. We are warriors fighting unjust and corrupt government prosecutions with a history of success and a reputation for tenacity, courage and legal ingenuity.

Our firm provides experienced legal support in all types of DWI cases across the Dallas – Fort Worth area and throughout Texas. We understand how stressful it is to face charges that threaten your license suspension, your freedom, and your future.

Our Dallas DWI attorneys have beat DWI breath scores, blood scores, and field sobriety tests. Let us handle your case, and we will take care of everything from your driver’s license privileges to creating a formidable strategy to get your case completely dismissed or the most favorable outcome possible.

If the police arrested you for DWI in Dallas, you may reasonably worry about what you can do to fight your case. Suppose you took a breathalyzer or blood test, and the sample tested for a blood alcohol concentration (BAC) greater than the legal limit of .08. In that case, you might think that there is nothing you can do to fight these charges. But you would be wrong.

Whether you failed a breath test, blood test or the roadside field sobriety tests, a seasoned Dallas DWI attorney can utilize many of the best defense strategies to beat the scores in your defense. You need someone who understands what you are going through and can fight for your freedom. When facing a DWI case, an experienced DWI attorney on your side will make all the difference.

Do you need a Dallas DWI attorney? Call us today at (888) 239-9305 to discuss legal representation.

Contact Us Online 24/7

What Is the Legal definition of a DWI Offense in Texas?

In Texas, a person commits the criminal offense of DWI by operating a motor vehicle in a public place while intoxicated.

The legal definition of “intoxicated” includes having a blood alcohol concentration (BAC) of 0.08 or more, or not having the normal use of mental or physical faculties due to alcohol, drugs, or any other substance. The Texas Penal Code outlines these definitions, and courts throughout Dallas County and across the state rely on these standards in criminal defense cases involving DWI criminal law.

How a Defense Lawyer Can Get a DWI Charge Dropped

In order to get a a DWI charge dropped, you must convince the state that they cannot prove at least one of the elements of the offense as it is defined in Penal Code §49.04.[1] Our lawyers are experts in Texas DWI law, and we leverage our legal knowledge to mount successful defenses to government prosecutions.

Our deep understanding of the Texas law regarding DWI helps us aggressively defend you in court. Our attorneys publish and regularly update a resource guide about every crime in the state of Texas, including a detailed analysis of the DWI statute in Texas.

How Do Defense Lawyers beat a DWI Case in Texas?

At our law office, we fight DWI prosecutions by building a strong defense that targets weaknesses in the prosecution’s case. This may involve challenging the breath or blood collection procedures or analysis, exposing errors made by the arresting officer, or attacking the basis for the initial stop if there was no reasonable suspicion or probable cause.

Your attorney must understand forensic science to challenge scientific evidence and confront expert witnesses on cross-examination. Blood and breath test scores mean nothing without proper analysis.

Building a Winning Strategy

Clients frequently ask whether we can beat certain test scores. The fact is that we regularly beat cases with high breath and blood test scores. Many factors can affect the validity and meaning of all BAC tests.

However, not all cases come down to testing protocols and challenging blood and breath evidence. Sometimes cases come down to whether the police violated your constitutional rights. Others come down to SFST testing. All cases are unique, but we always begin with the aim of getting your DWI charge dismissed. Unlike some other attorneys, we do not recycle one-size-fits-all tactics like personal injury practices.

DWI Defense usually boils down to attacking the state’s evidence on one or more of the following fronts:

  • Scientifically Unsound Blood Test or Breath Test Results
  • Fluctuating Alcohol Levels
  • No Probable Cause for Arrest
  • Failure to Obtain a Warrant

As experienced attorneys who have handled many intoxication offenses, including DWI 2nd, DWI 3rd, repeat felony DWI, and DWI accident cases, we provide our clients with the aggressive representation necessary to protect your rights and fight your case.

Why Choose Saputo Toufexis?

We are not former prosecutors, have never worked for the government and never will. We are defense lawyers who stake our reputation on bringing the fight to the government. We have earned our reputation as one of the best lawyers for DWI defense in the Dallas – Fort Worth area.

We don’t just practice law—we prepare each case to win. If you’re looking for a firm with a record of success and a commitment to results, contact us for a free consultation.

What Should You Do after a DWI in Dallas, TX?

After a DWI arrest in Texas, you must act quickly to preserve your rights and prevent a license suspension. You’ll receive notice of upcoming court dates, and missing one could result in a warrant and jail time. Contacting a law office focused on criminal defense should be your first step. The sooner a criminal defense attorney begins work on your case, the better your chances of avoiding a conviction.

Our firm represents people facing DWIs in Dallas County and surrounding areas, including Collin County and Denton County. We understand how the local criminal justice system operates and what legal specialization means in these high-stakes misdemeanor cases. The Texas board does not yet have a national college board certified DWI lawyer accreditation yet, but when you want to know who can handle these legal issues – look at the results.

How Do Criminal Defense Attorneys Challenge breath or blood Test Results?

DWI attorneys often challenge blood alcohol testing by questioning the validity of the procedures used or the qualifications of the arresting officer. At our law firm, we use strategies rooted in both science and courtroom experience. As active members of the Texas legal community, our highly trained criminal defense attorneys analyze every detail of the case. In Texas, the law office you choose can make all the difference when it comes to defeating unreliable breath or blood test results.

Breath and blood evidence can be challenged just like any other forensic claim—yet it requires a deeper knowledge of toxicology and constitutional law. Unlike personal injury cases that rarely turn on scientific nuance, DWI defense often comes down to a single blood draw. Informed cross-examination of lab technicians can be critical in securing an acquittal or dismissal.

What Are the Legal consequences of a Conviction for Drunk Driving?

In Texas, a DWI conviction can lead to license suspension, administrative license revocation, mandatory jail time, fines, probation, and community service. Our law office provides DWI defense to clients who need experienced legal representation and a deep understanding of the legal specialization involved in these cases.

A criminal defense attorney may also help you avoid harsh sentencing by negotiating alternatives such as deferred adjudication. Penalties increase for a second DWI offense and third or more (repeat) DWI and may include ignition interlock device requirements and mandatory treatment.

You may also be required to attend a court-ordered DWI education class as a condition of probation. Our DWI attorneys help you prepare for every aspect of sentencing, including administrative penalties under Texas law. If you’re concerned about your future and want clarity on what you’re facing, contact our team for a free consultation. We’ll help you understand your legal options and begin building a defense plan designed to minimize consequences and preserve your rights.

What Are the types of DWI Charges in Texas?

In Texas, a simple DWI is classified as a Class B misdemeanor. But that is just one of the intoxication offenses. Outlined in Chapter 49 of the Texas Penal Code, other criminal DWI charges include:

  • DWI 2nd
  • Felony DWI (repeat – 3rd offense or more)
  • Driving While Intoxicated With Child Passenger
  • Flying While Intoxicated
  • Boating While Intoxicated
  • Boating While Intoxicated with Child Passenger
  • Assembling or Operating an Amusement Park Ride While Intoxicated
  • Intoxication Assault
  • Intoxication Manslaughter
  • Driving or Operating Watercraft Under the Influence of Alcohol by a Minor (“DUI“)

Four scenarios can result in a felony DWI or intoxication charge:

  • After two DWI convictions, the state convicts you of a third or subsequent DWI.
  • You caused a non-fatal injury in an accident while operating a motor vehicle while intoxicated. If any party was seriously injured, the state will charge this as Intoxication Assault, a third-degree felony in Texas.
  • You caused a death in an accident caused by your drunk driving. The state will charge this offense as Intoxication Manslaughter, a second-degree felony.
  • You had a child in your car or boat while driving under the influence. If the child was younger than 15, the state will charge this as a Driving While Intoxicated With Child Passenger or Boating While Intoxicated with Child Passenger, both state jail felonies.

What Happens to your Driver’s License at a Dallas ALR Hearing and Why Does It Matter?

At your ALR hearing, the Texas Department of Public Safety will attempt to suspend your driver’s license through the administrative license revocation process. Although this is separate from the criminal court case, the stakes are still high. If you lose, the penalties can include long-term license suspension and other severe penalties that affect your livelihood.

Our lawyers prepare DWI defense strategies to fight these cases aggressively. We help clients in Dallas County challenge license suspensions and protect their ability to drive legally under Texas law, including obtaining occupational licenses when necessary.

How Can a Defense Lawyer Help Protect Your Driving privileges?

A skilled DWI attorney can often prevent or reduce license suspension by requesting timely hearings and negotiating terms. At our law office, we help clients apply for occupational licenses and prepare them for ignition interlock device requirements. Whether you’re in Dallas County, Denton County, Collin County, or Fort Worth, our firm builds DWI defense strategies designed to protect your driving privileges and keep you on the road legally.

What Should You Expect at a Dallas DWI Arraignment or Criminal Defense Case hearing?

Your arraignment is the first formal court appearance, where you’ll hear the charges and enter a plea. A qualified criminal defense attorney will explain the process, help you prepare for your court dates, and appear on your behalf when possible. Our law office handles DWI cases in Dallas, Fort Worth, and surrounding jurisdictions.

Choosing the right experienced attorney matters. Our firm includes lawyers recognized by Texas Super Lawyers and consistently named among the best lawyers for DWI defense in the region. Whether you’re facing jail time or seeking to avoid a conviction, we will guide you through every stage with confidence and clarity.

What does an Indecent Assault charge really mean?

The general definition of the Texas charge of Indecent Assault, according to the Texas Penal Code, is as follows:

(a) A person commits an offense if, without the other person‘s consent and with the intent to arouse or gratify the sexual desire of any person, the person:

(1) touches the anus, breast, or any part of the genitals of another person;

(2) touches another person with the anus, breast, or any part of the genitals of any person;

(3) exposes or attempts to expose another person‘s genitals, pubic area, anus, buttocks, or female areola; or

(4) causes another person to contact the blood, seminal fluid, vaginal fluid, saliva, urine, or feces of any person.

Our firm has built a professional reputation for taking on the Dallas area legal system in allegations of a sensitive nature and defending people when their freedom is on the line. As an experienced criminal defense lawyer in Dallas, Paul Saputo understands the stakes in these cases. When you hire us as your Dallas Sexual Assault attorney, we fight to win. From the courtrooms of Dallas to the battleground of social media, we fight to clear your name and your record.

We’re not just Sexual Assault lawyers. We are warriors fighting unjust and corrupt government prosecutions with a history of success and a reputation for tenacity, courage and legal ingenuity.

When the state prosecutes you for Sexual Assault, both your freedom and your reputation are at risk. Consider the damage to your reputation, liability for a civil suit and the emotional pain and anger that comes just from the accusation!

Accordingly, the lawyers at Saputo Toufexis aim to not only win your case, but also keep your name out of the public eye to achieve real justice. As a result of pushing the envelope of criminal law for years, we have extensive experience in investigating sex crimes accusations and defending alleged offenders in court. We handle every aspect of your Sexual Assault representation, from defending you in the media, in court at pre-trial hearings, and all the way through trial.

Do you need a Dallas Sexual Assault attorney? Call us today at (888) 239-9305 to discuss legal representation.

Contact Us Online 24/7

How are Sexual Assault and Aggravated Sexual Assault defined under Texas law?

Understanding the Sexual Assault Statute

The Texas Penal Code defines Sexual Assault in broad and unforgiving terms. For cases involving adult victims, the statute focuses on nonconsensual sexual conduct involving penetration or contact without the person’s consent. A person commits sexual assault if the person intentionally or knowingly causes any kind of sexual penetration of another person without that person’s consent.

Importantly, consent under Texas law does not carry its ordinary dictionary meaning. For example, a person may be deemed incapable of consent due to intoxication, coercion, or authority imbalance—even if no overt force is used. Texas identifies fourteen distinct scenarios where consent is legally lacking, further complicating what may appear on the surface to be a consensual encounter.

Prosecutors often rely on strained theories to frame behavior as criminal, even where no physical evidence exists. That’s why the role of an attorney is critical. The law covers not only penetration, but also certain types of sexual acts that might not involve intercourse at all.

Sexual Assault of a Child

A person commits Child Sexual Assault by causing sexual penetration or certain kinds of sexual contact with a child. The law classifies any sexual offense involving a child under the age of 17 as a second-degree or first-degree felony depending on the conduct and the alleged victim’s age. These charges do not require the state to prove lack of a person’s consent, as the law presumes that minors are legally incapable of consenting to sexual conduct.

Additionally, if the alleged crime involves a child under 14 or the use of a deadly weapon, the charge may escalate to aggravated sexual assault, which carries a much steeper prison sentence and lifetime consequences. In fact, using a deadly weapon, threatening another person, or engaging in group acts may qualify the case as first degree felony conduct under the law.

Statutory Enhancements and Felony Levels

Depending on the specifics of the alleged offense, the state may charge an alleged offender with a third degree felony, a second degree felony, or a first degree felony. Each classification carries increasing penalties, with first degree felony charges involving life imprisonment or a minimum prison sentence of 25 years in certain cases involving younger children.

To make matters worse, the legal process does not require prosecutors to prove that the alleged offender knew the age of the child. Mistake-of-age defenses are not permitted, and courts have consistently upheld this strict liability approach.

How a Defense Lawyer Can Get a Sexual Assault Charge Dropped

In order to get a a Sexual Assault charge dropped, you must convince the state that they cannot prove at least one of the elements of the offense as it is defined in Penal Code §22.011.[1] Our lawyers are experts in Texas Sexual Assault law, and we leverage our legal knowledge to mount successful defenses to government prosecutions.

Our deep understanding of the Texas law regarding Sexual Assault helps us aggressively defend you in court. Our attorneys publish and regularly update a resource guide about every crime in the state of Texas, including a detailed analysis of the Sexual Assault statute in Texas.

What criminal charges and penalties can result from a Sexual Assault allegation?

Levels of Sexual Assault Charges Under Texas Law

A sexual assault charge can be classified as either a first or second degree felony. If the accusation involves a child under the age of 17, the charge automatically escalates in seriousness. If the victim is younger than 14—or if a deadly weapon was involved—the state may pursue an aggravated sexual assault charge, triggering an even longer time period of prison time.

Even when there’s no physical evidence, the mere accusation can lead to indictment. Once indicted, the case proceeds to formal prosecution in court. In Dallas County, sexual abuse cases are often fast-tracked for review by specialized units within the District Attorney’s Office.

Penalty Range for Sex Assault

A second degree felony conviction for sexual assault can result in a prison sentence of 2 to 20 years. When charged as a first degree, the punishment range expands to 5 to 99 years or life. In some aggravated sexual assault cases, the prison sentence carries a minimum term of 25 years if the victim is under six years old or if the conduct involved violence or a deadly weapon.

Collateral Consequences of a Conviction

The impact of a criminal charge for sexual assault goes well beyond court. Beyond incarceration, a person convicted of a sex crime may also face hefty fines, a requirement to register as a sex offender, and restrictions on where the person can live or work. A sex crime conviction can permanently alter a person’s status in society, even after time has been served.

For example, a family member of an alleged offender may seek to modify child possession or visitation based on the outcome of the criminal case in court. In addition, certain occupations will no longer be available to a person convicted of a sexual offense—particularly if the person’s case involves a child.

Some charges related to sexual misconduct, such as indecency with a child or sexual performance by a child, are often filed alongside sexual assault, compounding the legal exposure and punishment range. The long-term consequences are severe, especially when the government alleges that multiple victims were involved or that the crime was part of a pattern.

How does our law office defend clients accused of a serious sex crime?

Our Philosophy: Strategic, Relentless, and Proven

At Saputo Toufexis, our law office brings a trial-focused mindset to every case our attorneys take. Our team does not aim for fast pleas—we aim to win. With significant experience in criminal cases involving allegations of sexual abuse, we develop strategies rooted in constitutional protections, forensic scrutiny, and aggressive motion practice. Our experienced criminal defense lawyers fight for clients both in the courtroom and in the court of public opinion.

Investigative Approach and Evidence Suppression

Our attorneys conduct independent investigations to contest every factual assumption in the State’s case. We often consult digital forensic experts to uncover metadata that refutes timelines and contradicts the narratives of the alleged victim. If the case involves minors, our attorneys coordinate with professional interviewers to evaluate how the child was questioned and whether leading tactics were used. We challenge search warrants, cell tower pings, and chain of custody issues—whatever the facts allow.

Aggressive Defense Against Government Overreach

We understand the emotional and political weight that comes with sex crime allegations, especially when a person is falsely accused. These are not just legal matters—they’re existential threats to your life, family, and future. We’ve seen the State pursue cases where probable cause was flimsy at best, yet a guilty verdict would still destroy someone’s reputation, career, and destroy a person’s life.

Our attorneys have a proven track record of securing case dismissals, not-guilty verdicts, and strategic plea agreements. When we represent clients, we pursue justice by forcing the government to meet its burden or back down entirely.

What happens after a Dallas Sexual Assault arrest and how does the process unfold?

Initial Arrest and Bail Conditions

After a sexual assault arrest, law enforcement will transport the alleged offender to the county jail. The magistrate typically sets bail and imposes strict bond conditions—often including no contact with the alleged victim, travel restrictions, and even electronic monitoring. These terms can disrupt the person’s life immediately, even before the state presents any evidence.

Pre-Indictment Proceedings

During the early stages of the legal process, prosecutors evaluate whether they can proceed with formal criminal charges. If they believe they can prove the alleged offender committed the sexual abuse, they may present the case to a grand jury, which determines whether the alleged offense should proceed to indictment. In many sex crime cases, this decision is made quickly, and often without input from the defense.

How are alleged victim reports and statements handled in Sexual Assault cases?

Police Procedures and Interviews

In many sexual assault investigations, the entire case hinges on the statement of the alleged victim. Law enforcement may collect physical evidence, but more often, especially in cases involving children (like Indecency with a Child), the only proof is an outcry. These cases are sensitive by nature, but also prone to false accusations—particularly in the context of custody disputes or strained relationships with a family member.

Police often refer child complainants to forensic interview centers, where questioning is recorded. However, techniques used can sometimes lead the alleged victim to give coached or suggestive responses. This places the alleged offender in a nearly impossible position of disproving subjective claims, which are then passed on to prosecutors as fact.

Are child pornography charges sometimes filed with Dallas Sexual Assault cases?

Yes. It’s increasingly common for prosecutors to file these charges alongside a sexual assault allegation. In many cases involving a child or teen, police examine phones, computers, and cloud accounts for digital images or messages that might support a broader narrative of exploitation or abuse. Even when a defendant is not accused of distributing content, the crime of “possession” can be charged based on recovered media.

What should you do to protect your rights and pursue legal representation?

When facing a sexual assault investigation, your first priority should be to remain silent until you consult with legal counsel. Speaking to police without an experienced attorney can seriously damage your defense. Law enforcement already believes a crime occurred, and their questions are not neutral. Their goal is to build a case against an alleged offender—not to hear your side.

Preserving evidence, such as messages, photos, or contact logs, is critical. These materials may support your version of events and contradict the alleged victim’s claims. If you’re under investigation, seek legal representation immediately. An experienced Dallas sexual assault lawyer can intervene early and defend your constitutional rights from the very beginning. Your freedom—and your life—may depend on what you do in these first moments.

How do criminal defense strategies work in Dallas County Sexual Assault cases?

Every sexual abuse case in Dallas presents unique legal and factual issues. The DA’s office uses special units to prosecute sex crime allegations, often pushing for fast indictments and plea deals. As a result, building a strong defense requires a custom strategy.

Our team focuses on attacking weaknesses in the government’s evidence. We challenge search warrants, interrogate lab processes, and highlight inconsistencies in the victim’s story. In many criminal trials, jury selection is key—we seek panelists who will weigh facts fairly, not be swayed by emotion.

Why should you schedule a free consultation with a defense lawyer right away?

The consequences of a sexual offense conviction are severe and lasting. You may face prison time, sex offender registration, and complete loss of your career. Even third degree felony charges can result in incarceration and require you to register as a sex offender.

Don’t underestimate what’s at stake. A single misstep can lead to a guilty verdict that changes your life forever. You need a defense team with a professional reputation for excellence and a history of defending the accused with commitment and care. Call us now for a confidential consultation.

State, decided on June 23, 2022, by the Court of Appeals of Texas, Fifth District Dallas, Kenneth Said Cruz-Banegas was convicted of Continuous Sexual Abuse of a Young Child in Collin County. He received a sentence of thirty-three years’ imprisonment. Cruz-Banegas contended that the evidence was insufficient to support his conviction and that the trial court abused its discretion by denying his motion for mistrial based on a witness’s emotional outburst during testimony. The abuse included multiple acts of sexual misconduct against the complainant, S.D., while she was under fourteen years old, occurring over a period exceeding thirty days.

The court upheld the conviction, detailing the various incidents of abuse testified by S.D., who was seventeen at the time of the trial. S.D.’s testimony described inappropriate touching, penetration, and other acts of sexual abuse that started when she was in fifth grade. The evidence presented, including the forensic interviewer’s and a child abuse pediatrician’s testimonies, supported the jury’s verdict. The appellate court also addressed the motion for mistrial, which was raised due to an emotional outburst from the victim’s mother during her testimony. The court ruled that the outburst did not prejudice the fairness of the trial significantly enough to warrant a mistrial, as it was brief, and the mother composed herself quickly without further incident.

This case underscores the appellate court’s role in scrutinizing the sufficiency of the evidence in cases involving sexual abuse of minors and the handling of emotional outbursts during trial. By affirming the conviction, the court emphasized that the evidence was sufficient to support the jury’s findings and that procedural discretion was appropriately exercised by the trial court in denying the motion for mistrial. The decision illustrates the legal challenges involved in cases of continuous sexual abuse and the importance of maintaining procedural integrity in emotionally charged trials.

In another Collin County Continuous Sexual Abuse case, the Fifth District Court of Appeals reviewed a verdict from the 366th Judicial District Court Collin County. Subsequently, the appellate court filed an opinion on June 30, 2023, in the case styled The State of Texas v. Manuel Herrera in Cause No. 05-22-00015-CR.

The trial court otherwise denied appellant’s motion for directed verdict and, after appellant rested his case, charged the jury on Count 1 (continuous sexual abuse of a child), Count 3 (indecency with a child by contact), and Count 4 (aggravated sexual assault of a child). The jury found appellant guilty of each of the charged offenses, and the case proceeded to punishment before the court.

(B) a disabled individual.

The State of Texas v. Cyze Rodgers

The appellate court reported the background of the case as follows:

Appellant was indicted for attempted arson in June 2018. With the assistance of court-appointed counsel, appellant judicially confessed to the charge and entered into a plea agreement with the State. At a hearing on November 13, 2018, the trial court accepted the plea agreement and entered an order of deferred adjudication conditioned on his compliance with certain terms of community supervision. Among other things, the terms included that appellant must report to the Dallas County Community Supervision and Corrections Department (CSCD) when directed and “participate in a domestic violence treatment program (BIPP)” within sixty days from referral.

At the end of the hearing, the trial court found that appellant violated the terms of his community supervision, adjudicated him guilty, and orally sentenced him to two years’ confinement. The same day, the trial court entered its judgment adjudicating guilt. This appeal followed.

(a) A person commits an offense if, with specific intent to commit an offense, he does an act amounting to more than mere preparation that tends but fails to effect the commission of the offense intended.

(b) If a person attempts an offense that may be aggravated, his conduct constitutes an attempt to commit the aggravated offense if an element that aggravates the offense accompanies the attempt.

Murder charges in Texas also apply under the state’s new fentanyl law when a person supplies drugs that result in death.

Other charges involving the death of another person include intoxication manslaughter, involuntary manslaughter, and voluntary manslaughter. These offenses reflect different mental states, from intent to criminal negligence, and each is charged and punished differently under Texas law. Manslaughter requires the state to prove a person recklessly took another human life, such as in a fatal accident. Criminally negligent homicide applies when a person causes death by failing to act with reasonable care, even if they did not intend to cause harm.

It’s essential to understand that assault with a Aggravated Assault with a Deadly Weapon Injury isn’t limited to situations where a gun is shown or fired. According to Texas Penal Code § 1.07, a deadly weapon includes firearms, any object designed to cause death or serious injury, or any item capable of inflicting death or severe bodily injury. If such an item is used during an assault, the individual may face Aggravated Assault with a Deadly Weapon Injury charges.

An Assault offense is also elevated to Aggravated Assault when serious bodily injury results.

In Texas, there is no distinct statute for battery; assault and battery are charged under a single statute. However, that’s not the case everywhere. In some states, the two crimes are charged separately.

What happens at a Tarrant County arraignment?

At your arraignment, a Tarrant County judge will hear your plea of not guilty. In Tarrant County, you may not have an attorney at your initial arraignment. However, the court will not hear a guilty plea prior to your being represented by counsel. In addition, the court may also set bail and bond conditions if you have not already received them.

If the police have arrested you for Aggravated Assault, then Texas Code of Criminal Procedure §17.40 requires Tarrant County judges to “impose any reasonable condition of bond related to the safety of a victim of the alleged offense or to the safety of the community” to secure your attendance at trial. If the state alleges that you violated those bond conditions, then the Tarrant County Sheriff’s Office can immediately return you to custody. Accordingly, judges have very broad power in determining bail conditions and bond amounts.

What is the most common sentence for Tarrant County Aggravated Assault charge in Tarrant County?

The Texas Penal Code defines the penalty range for Aggravated Assault offenses across Texas. The Penal Code classifies the punishment for Aggravated Assault as a second or third degree felony, depending on the circumstances. However, it is important to consider the potential collateral consequences of a Aggravated Assault conviction. These collateral consequences are additional penalties not directly outlined in the penal code’s penalty scheme, but nonetheless accompany the conviction. Your Tarrant County Aggravated Assault attorney should discuss these consequences with you before you decide how to handle your case.

The exact penalty one might face from a Aggravated Assault conviction varies greatly, influenced by factors such as you prior criminal record and the offense specifics. You can find details on the penalty range for all Aggravated Assault here. For specifics on typical penalties in Tarrant County Aggravated Assault cases, call us to schedule a consultation or book a consultation online.

Collateral Consequences for All Felony Convictions

If you are convicted of a felony, you will be labeled as a convicted felon for the remainder of your natural life. You will lose certain civil rights, such as the right to vote (see Texas Election Code §11.002(4)) and the right to possess ammunition or firearms (18 U.S.C. §922(g) and Texas Penal Code §46.04).

The felony conviction also makes it difficult to gain and maintain employment and may result in an individual’s loss of ability to be licensed in certain professions. Convicted felons also lose their ability to join and served in the country’s armed forces.

What is first degree felony Aggravated Assault?

In some instances, aggravated assault can be elevated from a second-degree to a first-degree felony. Punishments at this level are much more severe, including a prison sentence ranging from 5 to 99 years and/or a fine of up to $10,000.

Aggravated Assault as a First Degree Felony

Aggravated assault is considered a first degree felony when:

  • A deadly weapon is used to cause serious bodily injury to a family or household member, or a dating partner;
  • It’s committed by a public servant in the course of their official duties;
  • It’s committed against an on-duty public servant or security officer;
  • It’s committed as retaliation against a witness, prospective witness, informant, or person who reported a crime;
  • It involves discharging a firearm from a vehicle, resulting in serious bodily injury to another person.

What kinds of weapons are typically used in Aggravated Assault charges?

Aggravated Assault with a Deadly Weapon charges require the state to prove the use of a deadly weapon. According to the Texas Penal Code, deadly weapons are defined broadly. Deadly weapons frequently used in Aggravated Assault cases in Texas include:

  • Firearms
  • Vehicles
  • An explosive weapon
  • Machine gun
  • Short-barrel firearm
  • Armor-piercing ammunition
  • Chemical dispensing device
  • Zip gun
  • Switchblade knife
  • Knuckles
  • Club
  • Blackjack
  • Nightstick
  • Mace
  • Tomahawk
  • Handgun
  • Knife
  • Dagger
  • Bowie knife
  • Sword
  • Spear
  • Illegal knife

How to defend domestic or family violence Aggravated Assault cases?

Domestic violence allegations can sometimes be baseless accusations arising from marriages headed toward divorce or child custody disputes. In other cases, both parties may share the blame. Many counties have grant-funded domestic violence divisions with specially trained prosecutors, investigators, and victim advocates. While these individuals mean well, many become “true believers” who assume your guilt. Often, only a jury trial acquittal can change their minds.

In many cases, the victim or reporting person changes their mind but learns too late that the government can still prosecute despite their objections, even after filing an affidavit of non-prosecution. These individuals don’t realize that the prosecutor is more concerned with why they want to drop charges than the fact that they do. My job is to investigate the relationship history, incident details, and characteristics of the parties involved. In some cases, one or more of these factors can lead to dropped charges or significantly reduced penalties, especially if the victim does not want to proceed. There’s no universal formula; it takes my expertise to identify potential defenses and ways to improve your situation.

Domestic violence crimes include Assault Family Violence, Aggravated Assault Family Violence, Harassment, Stalking, Violation of a Protective Order, and Assault Family Violence Enhanced to Felony (due to previous convictions). A determined accuser can create a complex web that can be difficult to escape. My experience prosecuting and defending these crimes benefits my clients. Crafting a defense for a complex situation requires knowledge and experience, and I possess both, having successfully done it repeatedly.

Continuous family violence and assault impeding charges are the latest offenses in this area. They can quickly escalate the most absurd situations into serious felonies, threatening everything important to my clients. I have in-depth knowledge of self-defense laws and the complex rules of character evidence, which come into play in almost all these cases. The courtroom is not a place for mudslinging; most bad character evidence is inadmissible unless a firmly rooted exception applies. Few lawyers have my level of expertise in these areas, allowing me to present evidence that truly matters before the jury.

Even if you’re guilty, punishments recommended by the government, even probation, can be excessive with lifetime implications. I always explore every option to reduce or eliminate any loss of freedom. Pre-trial diversions, conditional dismissals, batterer’s intervention, anger management, alcohol and drug treatment, or pleading to a lesser charge (like Class C Assault-Offensive Contact or Disorderly Conduct) are all possibilities in domestic violence cases.

In some instances, only a complete dismissal of charges or an acquittal will suffice.

Are you under investigation for Aggravated Assault? Should you cooperate with the police investigation?

We have assisted our clients through many difficult police interrogations. Although we do not always recommend consenting to an interrogation, occasionally we recognize circumstances where consenting to an interrogation may serve your best interest. However, you should never do a police interview without your Tarrant County Aggravated Assault lawyer present.

An arrest for Aggravated Assault can drastically change your life, even if a court dismisses your case. Do not hesitate to contact us immediately if you are under investigation.

In some cases we have communicated directly with law enforcement authorities on behalf of our clients instead of consenting to a direct interrogation. In general, we recommend avoiding police interrogations because of the extreme level of stress that you will likely experience. Even if you are innocent, the Tarrant County police and the community will likely judge the way you act and what you say negatively. We must carefully consider this because this negative perception will almost certainly impact your final case disposition. As your Tarrant County Aggravated Assault attorney, we can assist you in these difficult circumstances.

What does a Continuous Smuggling charge really mean?

The Texas Penal Code defines the charge of Continuous Smuggling as follows:

(a) A person commits an offense if, during a period that is 10 or more days in duration, the person engages two or more times in conduct that constitutes an offense under Section 20.05.

Can the police can charge multiple individuals in the same car?

Yes, the police can charge multiple individuals involved in the same car if they are believed to have alternated driving duties in the same smuggling operation.

Only lawyers with the highest ethical standards and professional ability receive this Martindale-Hubbell Peer Review Rating.

Martindale-Hubbell awarded attorney Paul Saputo the “Client Champion” award. From Martindale:

Martindale-Hubbell’s new Client Champion awards recognize those attorneys who excel at service as affirmed by their clients. The awards, based on the quantity and quality of an attorney’s Martindale-Hubbell client reviews, demonstrate an ongoing commitment to delivering excellent client service.

Best Lawyers selected Mr. Saputo as a “Ones to Watch” in the White Collar Attorney practice area. Paul Saputo has also been named to the Texas Super Lawyers list. In addition, Paul Saputo has been selected in consecutive years to D Magazine’s Best Lawyers: Criminal Defense list and D Magazine’s Best Lawyers Under 40.

Paul Saputo has also achieved a perfect “10.0 – Top Attorney” rating on AVVO, multiple AVVO “Client’s Choice” awards and a “10.0” rating on Justia.

Since 2018, attorney Paul Saputo has also been awarded the “Best Business: Three Best Rated®” distinction. 

Background & Training

Mr. Saputo has practiced throughout Texas in more than fifty Texas state and federal courts. He has obtained hundreds of dismissals and acquittals for clients facing a wide array of serious charges. He has also developed groundbreaking innovations in defense strategies and tactics.

A member of the prestigious Texas Bar College, he continues to both train other lawyers in various continuing education seminars and attend many hours of continuous legal education on a yearly basis with some of the best lawyers, judges and law professors in the country. Mr. Saputo has delivered seminars on topics including “Legislative Updates,” “Advanced Record Clearing,” and other hot topics in criminal law. He is dedicated to defending people accused of crimes and courageously standing up to fight the government when lives and freedom are in jeopardy.

Mr. Saputo is a graduate of the elite Duke University School of Law, a nationally recognized top-ten law school in the United States. Before graduating law school, he worked for a Federal District Court Judge and wrote several appellate briefs for defendants in California challenging the medical marijuana laws of that state.

After law school, Mr. Saputo worked as an attorney at the internationally renowned law firm of Vinson & Elkins, LLP. While there Mr. Saputo helped represent some of the largest companies in the world and received high-level legal training. After leaving Vinson & Elkins, he worked for and with several of the leading criminal defense attorneys in the state of Texas before he founded the firm.

Now he brings his high-level legal training and experience to each one of his clients’ cases. And above all, his commitment to zealously representing his clients in court drives him to the great degree of success that he enjoys in the practice of criminal defense law.

Mr. Saputo is proud to represent some of the best clients in world. He is a deeply passionate attorney who believes that a fair trial is something that must be won through aggressive legal representation. While the process can be daunting, and in many ways unfair, he appreciates the opportunity to go to work for you and stand up for your rights – leveling the playing field and making sure that you are treated with the dignity and compassion that you deserve.

Memberships & Service

As an active member of many criminal defense organizations, Mr. Saputo maintains the highest level of professionalism, proficiency, knowledge and expertise in criminal law. He is a member of organizations including the Texas Bar Association, Texas Bar College, Dallas Criminal Defense Lawyers Association, Texas Criminal Defense Lawyers Association, the DUI Defense Lawyers Association, the Tarrant County Criminal Defense Lawyers Association and the Dallas Bar Association, among others.

Mr. Saputo currently is a past director and secretary of the Dallas Criminal Defense Lawyers Association.

We are active in many criminal defense and legal organizations, and we regularly contribute to the advancement of the criminal defense legal representation. Attorney Paul Saputo regularly presents continuing education seminars to other lawyers, judges and academics.

Bar & Court Admissions

Paul Saputo is admitted to practice in the following courts:

  • All District Courts in Texas
  • All County Courts in Texas
  • The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals & The Texas Supreme Court
  • All Texas Courts of Appeal
  • The United States Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals
  • The United States District Court for the Northern District of Texas
  • The United States District Court for the Western District of Texas
  • The United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas
  • The United States District Court for the Western District of Oklahoma

Paul Saputo’s Texas Bar Association profile

More about Paul Saputo here >

About Nicholas Toufexis

Nick Toufexis
Managing Partner

Awards & Recognition

Mr. Toufexis was awarded the Texas Super Lawyers Rising Stars award.

Background & Training

Mr. Toufexis is a veteran of the United States Navy and after serving for 10 years, he has brought that same tenacity to his legal career. As a combat veteran, Mr. Toufexis has used his experiences and translated that fighting attitude to the courtroom. Even before going to law school, Mr. Toufexis knew that his passion was fighting for the rights of the accused and has shown that passion through the exceptional results he has achieved in court. His “think outside the box” mentality has turned many negatives in cases into positives.

Mr. Toufexis believes that everyone is deserving of tenacious legal representation, and that everyone deserves their day in court. Mr. Toufexis is passionate about protecting the rights of the accused and has shown through his actions that he is willing to stand up for their rights.
 
Mr. Toufexis is ready to go to work for you and ensure that your rights and freedoms are fully protected.
 
Mr. Toufexis is a member of the prestigious Texas Bar College, and he continues to better himself through numerous hours of continuous legal education, attending some of the most sought-after education from some of the best lawyers in Texas.
 
Mr. Toufexis is a graduate of Southern Methodist University in Dallas, Texas. During law school, Mr. Toufexis worked as an intern for Mr. Saputo, learning how to not only defend clients, but attack the prosecutions case. After law school, Mr. Toufexis went to work as a licensed attorney for the firm. After working with Mr. Saputo for years, Mr. Toufexis was named a partner in the Saputo Toufexis Criminal Defense firm.

Memberships & Service

Mr. Toufexis serves as the co-chair for the Solo and Small Firms committee in the Dallas Association of Young Lawyers and is an active member in the Texas Criminal Defense Lawyers Association, Dallas Criminal Defense Lawyers Association and Texas Bar Association.

Mr. Toufexis was awarded Dallas Association of Young Lawyers “One to Watch” for February 2023.

Mr. Toufexis has also been published in Headnotes for his article “Spoliation in Criminal Law” and is continuing to write articles not only for other lawyers to read and learn, but also for the general public to help them better understand the law.

Bar & Court Admissions

Nick Toufexis is admitted to practice in the following courts:

  • All District Courts in Texas
  • All County Courts in Texas
  • The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals & The Texas Supreme Court
  • All Texas Courts of Appeal
  • The United States Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals
  • The United States District Court for the Northern District of Texas
  • The United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas

More about Nicholas Toufexis here >

Hire the Firm

We know that when you need us, you are going through a traumatic experience, and we understand how important it is to you to have an attorney who will zealously represent you inside and outside of court. We understand that every aspect of your life may be in jeopardy, and we are here to help. When you become a client, you can leave your worry with us – we handle every aspect of your case. We strive to make sure you understand the entire process and all of the options that may be available to you.

Whether you have been arrested, charged or are under investigation, contact us immediately to protect your rights. The process is simple: book an appointment with us and tell us about your case in person or over the phone. If we agree to accept you as a client, we will quote you a fee and send you a contract to sign.

Please do not send the firm any confidential information about any matter until you receive a written or electronic notice from the firm advising you that the firm represents you (an “engagement letter”). When you receive an engagement letter from the firm, you will be the firm’s client, and we may exchange confidential information freely.

The firm accepts all forms of payment, including credit and debit cards, cash and checks.

Payment plans are welcome, and we also welcome active military and veterans with discounted rates.

When you hire Saputo Toufexis | Criminal Defense, our experienced criminal defense attorneys will review your case and analyze every detail to determine your best defense strategy. Whether we are representing you on a DWI charge, a possession of controlled substance case, a serious sex crime felony or in any other criminal prosecution, we conduct independent investigations, rigorously examine all the forensic evidence produced against you and advocate aggressively on your behalf.

item.content:encoded:
Dallas Criminal Defense Attorneys: Saputo | Toufexis

Among Texas cities, Dallas stands out as perhaps the most high-profile. Dallas criminal defense attorneys are among the best and most specialized in the state, owing at least in part to the city’s statewide and national prominence.

Based in Dallas, Texas, our firm has deep roots in the Dallas area. Attorneys Paul Saputo and Nick Toufexis both started their criminal defense careers in Dallas. The attorneys have long served the Dallas Criminal Defense Lawyers Association, and they have tried many cases in Dallas county.

DALLAS CRIMINAL DEFENSE ATTORNEY FAQs

  • What kinds of cases do our Dallas criminal defense attorneys handle?
  • How to choose a Dallas criminal defense attorney?
  • Where are the Dallas County Criminal Courts?
  • Where can I search for and find criminal cases in Dallas County?
  • Who are the Dallas Criminal Court judges? What courts are in Dallas County?

If you’re looking for the best Dallas criminal defense attorney, then we want to represent you.

At Saputo Toufexis | Criminal Defense, we are looking for clients who want to hire the top criminal defense attorneys in Dallas.

Our history of success in includes representation of numerous high-profile Dallas clients and notable high-profile victories. We have also disposed of many other cases quietly and out of the sight of the public. We use our experience to fight to keep all our clients out of Lew Sterrett and out of prison.

If you are looking for an authoritative Dallas criminal defense attorney, call us or book a consultation today.

What kinds of cases do our Dallas criminal defense attorneys handle?

  • Dallas Aggravated Assault Attorneys

How to choose a Dallas criminal defense attorney

It is not easy to find the best Dallas criminal defense attorney for your case. It’s difficult to even figure out where to start.

You can start by looking at reviews and testimonials, but as everyone knows these days, so much of that can be fake, purchased, or misleading.

It’s important to consider experience, but remember that lots of experience can sometimes lead to stagnation, carelessness, and cynicism.

You should consider reputation, but remember that some of the best criminal defense attorneys challenge the status quo in court, and this can result in them not being very popular.

There’s no magic recipe for what makes the best attorney for your case, so we suggest you talk to the attorneys and get a feel for where their passion lies. Are they passionate about criminal defense or did they just start doing this because they got kicked out of the Dallas DA’s office? Whose side is your attorney really on?

We have never worked as prosecutors. We have dedicated our entire legal careers to perfecting the art of Texas criminal defense. Learn more about us >

Where are the Dallas County Criminal Courts?

The Dallas County Criminal Courts are located inside of the Frank Crowley Criminal Justice Center located at 133 N Riverfront Blvd, Dallas, TX 75207.

Where can I search for and find criminal cases in Dallas County?

You can find records related to Dallas county criminal cases on the county’s case records page.

Who are the Dallas Criminal Court judges? What courts are in Dallas County?

Dallas County has 13 county criminal courts. These are the courts that handle most misdemeanor offenses. Dallas County has 17 district courts. These are the courts that handle felony offenses.

This list starts with the Dallas County misdemeanor courts. Jump to the felony courts.

Parker County Misdemeanor Courts

  • Criminal County Court 1 (MA Court).
    • A former Dallas criminal defense attorney, Judge Marilynn Mayse currently presides over Criminal County Court 1 in Dallas. Judge Mayse defeated Judge Dan Patterson in the Democratic primary in 2022 and won the general election for this court. Criminal County Court 1 is on the 3rd floor of the Frank Crowley Criminal Court Complex in Dallas.
  • Criminal County Court 2 (MB Court).
    • As of 2015, Judge Julia Hayes presides over Criminal County Court 2 in Dallas. Judge Hayes took the bench in 2010 after beating Republican Dan Motalvo in the general election. She is on the Democratic ticket. Criminal County Court 2 is on the 3rd floor of the Frank Crowley Criminal Court Complex in Dallas.
  • Criminal County Court 3 (MC Court).
    • Judge Audrey Moorehead presides over Criminal County Court 3 in Dallas. Judge Moorehead ran unopposed in the Democratic primary and eventually won her bench after defeating Symone Redwine in the general election in 2018. Criminal County Court 3 is on the 3rd floor of the Frank Crowley Criminal Court Complex in Dallas.
  • Criminal County Court 4 (ME Court)
    • Judge Dominique Torres Williams took the bench in 2023 after defeating Democratic party opponent Angel Mata in the primary. Criminal County Court 4 is on the 3rd floor of the Frank Crowley Criminal Court Complex in Dallas.
  • Criminal County Court 5 (MF Court)
    • Judge Lisa Green is also a newcomer to the bench, having been elected in 2014 to replace Judge Etta Mullin. Judge Green beat both Etta Mullin and Trey Bunch in the Democratic primary before beating Etta Mullin in a primary runoff. She then defeated Leah Lucius in a hotly contested general election. She attended St. Mary’s University for both college and law school. Criminal County Court 5 is on the 3rd floor of the Frank Crowley Criminal Court Complex in Dallas.
  • Criminal County Court 6 (MG Court)
    • Judge King has presided over Criminal County Court 6 in Dallas since 2006. Most recently she was re-elected in 2014. Criminal County Court 6 is on the 3rd floor of the Frank Crowley Criminal Court Complex in Dallas.
  • Criminal County Court 7 (MH Court)
    • Judge Remeko Edwards presides over Dallas’s Criminal County Court 7. She recently ran and won an unopposed election in both the primary and general election in 2022. Criminal County Court 7 is on the 4th floor of the Frank Crowley Criminal Court Complex in Dallas.
  • Criminal County Court 8 (MJ Court)
    • Another former Dallas criminal defense attorney, Judge Carmen White also ran and won an unopposed election in both the primary and general election in 2022. Criminal County Court 8 is on the 4th floor of the Frank Crowley Criminal Court Complex in Dallas.
  • Criminal County Court 9 (MK Court)
    • Judge Peggy Hoffman presides over Criminal County Court 9 in Dallas. She defeated Republican Leigh Logan in 2010 and has maintained her bench ever since. Criminal County Court 9 is on the 4th floor of the Frank Crowley Criminal Court Complex in Dallas.
  • Criminal County Court 10 (ML Court)
    • Judge Monique J. Huff presides over Criminal County Court 10 in Dallas. She defeated Elissa Wev and Etta Mullin in the Democratic primary. Criminal County Court 10 is on the 4th floor of the Frank Crowley Criminal Court Complex in Dallas.
  • Criminal County Court 11 (MN Court)
    • Judge Shequitta Kelly presides over Criminal County Court 11 in Dallas. Judge Kelly defeated Melodee Armstrong Mota in the primary election in 2014 before running unopposed in the general election in Dallas. Criminal County Court 11 is on the 4th floor of the Frank Crowley Criminal Court Complex in Dallas.
  • Criminal Court of Appeals 1 (MD Court)
    • Judge Kristin Wade presides over the Criminal Court of Appeals 1 in Dallas. Judge Wade has held the bench since 1999 and was most recently re-elected in 2014. She attended Trinity University and the SMU Dedman School of Law. Criminal Court of Appeals 1 is on the 3rd floor of the Frank Crowley Criminal Court Complex in Dallas.
  • Criminal Court of Appeals 2 (MM Court).
    • Judge Pamela Luther presides over the Criminal Court of Appeals 2 in Dallas. She has held the bench since 2019, after defeating Marilynn Mayse, Johnny Lanzillo IV, and Bruce Kaye in the Democratic primary. Criminal Court of Appeals 2 is on the 3rd floor of the Frank Crowley Criminal Court Complex in Dallas.

Dallas County Felony Courts

  • Criminal District Court 1 (FH Court)
    • Judge Tina Clinton presides over Criminal District Court 1 in Dallas. She took over the bench in 2019 after defeating Monique Ward in the primary. Criminal District Court 1 is on the 6th floor of the Frank Crowley Criminal Court Complex in Dallas.
  • Criminal District Court 2 (FI Court)
    • Judge JJ Koch presides over Criminal District Court 2 in Dallas. Judge Koch was appointed to the bench in 2023. Criminal District Court 2 is on the 7th floor of the Frank Crowley Criminal Court Complex in Dallas.
  • Criminal District Court 3 (FJ Court)
    • Judge Audra Riley presides over Criminal District Court 3 in Dallas. Judge Riley took the bench in 2021 after defeating Teresa Hawthorne in the primary. Criminal District Court 3 is on the 6th floor of the Frank Crowley Criminal Court Complex in Dallas.
  • Criminal District Court 4 (FK Court)
    • Judge Dominique Collins was elected to take the bench of Criminal District Court 4 in 2012. Judge Collins has served in the United States Air Force and has extensive experience in the Dallas County District Attorney’s Office. Criminal District Court 4 is on the 6th floor of the Frank Crowley Criminal Court Complex in Dallas. Judge Collins is a former Assistant District Attorney and former U.S. Air Force member. She also has recently revamped the Dallas Veteran’s Court Program.
  • Criminal District Court 5 (FL Court)
    • Judge Carter Thompson was re-elected in 2014. He ran unopposed in the Democratic primary and in the general election. Criminal District Court 5 is on the 5th floor of the Frank Crowley Criminal Court Complex in Dallas.
  • Criminal District Court 6 (FX Court)
    • Judge Nancy Mulder presides over Criminal District Court 6 took over this bench in 2023. She was previously the judge of County Criminal Court 4. Criminal District Court 6 is on the 6th floor of the Frank Crowley Criminal Court Complex in Dallas.
  • Criminal District Court 7 (FY Court)
    • Judge Chika Anyiam presides over Criminal District Court 7 in Dallas. She took the bench in 2019. Criminal District Court 7 is on the 7th floor of the Frank Crowley Criminal Court Complex in Dallas.
  • 194th Judicial District Court (FM Court)
    • Judge Ernest White sits on the bench of the 194th Judicial District Court. Texas’s 194th Judicial District Court is on the 7th floor of the Frank Crowley Criminal Court Complex in Dallas.
  • 195th Judicial District Court (FN Court)
    • Judge Hector Garza presides over the 195th Judicial District Court in Dallas. He was elected to the bench in 2015 after beating Republican civil attorney Mike Lee in the general election. Judge Garza bested a wide array of hopefuls in the Democratic primary. He has been on the bench ever since. Judge Fred Tinsley retired from this bench in July of 2015. Texas’s 195th Judicial District Court is on the 7th floor of the Frank Crowley Criminal Court Complex in Dallas.
  • 203rd Judicial District Court (FP Court)
    • Judge Raquel ‘Rocky’ Jones presides over the 203rd Judicial District Court. Judge Hawthorne was elected in 2018 after beating Teresa Hawthorne in the Democratic primary. Texas’s 203rd Judicial District Court is on the 7th floor of the Frank Crowley Criminal Court Complex in Dallas.
  • 204th Judicial District Court (FQ Court)
    • Judge Tammy Kemp presides over the 204th Judicial District Court. Judge Kemp ran against Lena Levario in the Democratic primary in 2014. She was unopposed in the general election, and has been on the bench ever since. Texas’s 204th Judicial District Court is on the 7th floor of the Frank Crowley Criminal Court Complex in Dallas.
  • 265th Judicial District Court (FR Court)
    • Judge Jennifer Bennett presides over the 265th Judicial District Court. Judge Bennett is a Democrat who ran against Anthony Eiland and William R. Barr in the 2014 primary before defeating Republican Lisa DeWitt in the Dallas general election. She has remained on the bench ever since. Texas’s 265th Judicial District Court is on the 7th floor of the Frank Crowley Criminal Court Complex in Dallas.
  • 282nd Judicial District Court (FS Court)
    • Judge Amber Givens-Davis was first elected to the bench of the 282nd Judicial District Court in 2014. She took office January 1, 2015. Texas’s 282nd Judicial District Court is on the 5th floor of the Frank Crowley Criminal Court Complex in Dallas.
  • 283rd Judicial District Court (FT Court)
    • Judge Lawrence Mays was first elected in 2018. Texas’s 283rd Judicial District Court is on the 6th floor of the Frank Crowley Criminal Court Complex in Dallas.
  • 291st Judicial District Court (FU Court)
    • Judge Stephanie Huff took office in 2019 after running unopposed. Texas’s 291st Judicial District Court is on the 7th floor of the Frank Crowley Criminal Court Complex in Dallas.
  • 292nd Judicial District Court (FV Court)
    • Judge Brandon Birmingham was elected judge of the 292nd Judicial District Court in 2014 after running against Larry Mitchell in the Democratic primary and later defeating Janet Cook in the general election. He attended Baylor for college before graduating from the University of South Texas College of Law. The 292nd Judicial District Court is on the 6th floor of the Frank Crowley Criminal Court Complex in Dallas.
  • 363rd Judicial District Court (FW Court)
    • Judge Tracy Holmes presides over the 363rd Judicial District Court. She competed against and defeated Nigel H. Redmond in the 2014 Democratic primary, and she has been on the bench ever since. The 363rd Judicial District Court is on the 5th floor of the Frank Crowley Criminal Court Complex in Dallas.

It is not easy to find the best Collin County criminal defense attorney for your case. It’s difficult to even figure out where to start.

It’s important to consider experience, but remember that lots of experience can sometimes lead to stagnation, carelessness, and cynicism.

This list starts with the Collin County misdemeanor courts. Jump to the felony courts.

Collin County Misdemeanor Courts

  • County Court at Law 1
    • Judge Corinne A. Mason currently presides over County Court at Law 1 in Collin County. Judge Mason ran unopposed as a Republican in 2010 to take the general election for this court. She has maintained this bench ever since.
  • County Court at Law 2
    • Judge Barnett Walker currently presides over County Court at Law 2 in Collin County. Judge Barnett Walker ran unopposed as a Republican in 2014 to take the general election for this court. He was re-elected in 2022 and his term expires in 2026.
  • County Court at Law 3
    • Judge Lance S. Baxter currently presides over County Court at Law 3 in Collin County. Judge Lance S. Baxter was elected to this court in 2010. He was re-elected in 2022 and his term expires in 2026.
  • County Court at Law 4
    • Judge David Rippel currently presides over County Court at Law 4 in Collin County. Judge David Rippel was elected to this court in 2010. Rippel, a Republican, beat a Democrat for the bench in 2010. He was re-elected in 2022 and his term expires in 2026.

  • 429th District Court
    • Judge Jill Renfro Willis presides over Texas’s Criminal 429th District Court. She ran unopposed in 2010 under the Republican ticket and has won every re-election since. Her current term expires in 2026.
  • 468th District Court
    • Judge Lindsey Wynne presides over Texas’s Criminal 468th District Court. She assumed office in 2019 and is up for reelection in 2024.
  • 469th District Court
    • Judge Piper McCraw presides over Texas’s Criminal 469th District Court. The 469th district court is a family court that was made in 2015. Judge McCraw is a Republican who was appointed by Governor Greg Abbott in 2015. She is up for reelection in 2024.
  • 470th District Court
    • Judge Brook Fulks presides over Texas’s Criminal 470th District Court. He was appointed to the court by Governor Greg Abbott in 2023. He is running for reelection in 2024.
  • 471st District Court
    • Judge Andrea K. Bouressa presides over Texas’s Criminal 471st District Court. She took office in 2019 after being appointed by Governor Greg Abbott. She is up for reelection in 2024.
  • 493rd District Court
    • Judge Christine A. Nowak presides over Texas’s Criminal 493rd District Court. She was appointed to the bench by Governor Greg Abbott in 2023. She is up for reelection in 2024.

Denton County Misdemeanor Courts

    • Judge Lauri Ragland presides over County Criminal Court 2 in Denton County. She ran unopposed in the Republican primary and won the general election in 2022. County Criminal Court 1 is located on the 1st floor of the Denton County Courts Building. Her current term ends in 2026.

  • 462nd District Court
    • Judge Lee Ann Breading presides over the 462nd District Court in Denton County. She was appointed to the court by Governor Greg Abbott in 2018. She won the Republican primary election in 2024 unopposed and will be on the ballot for the general election in November 2024.
  • 467th District Court

How do I get an Indecency With a Child charge dropped in Dallas, Texas?

In order to get an Indecency With a Child charge dropped in Dallas, you must convince the state that they cannot prove at least one of the elements of the offense as it is defined in Penal Code §21.11.[1] Our lawyers are experts in the Texas law regarding Indecency With a Child, and we leverage our legal knowledge to mount successful defenses to government prosecutions.

Thoroughly understanding both the Indecency With a Child statute and related case law contributes to effectively defending you in court. As part of our practice, we publish and regularly update a statutory resource guide covering all Texas Penal Code crimes. We analyze the Indecency With a Child statute in detail on the Indecency With a Child offense page. We also maintain our expertise by keeping up with the latest case law affecting Indecency With a Child cases in Dallas.

One such case is Bush v. State.

Bush v. State

In Bush v. State, the Court of Appeals of Texas Fifth District Dallas on March 27, 2020, reviewed the trial court’s judgment convicting Ronnie Bush of Indecency with a Child in Dallas County. Bush contended that the trial court improperly overruled his objections to the State’s expert witness testimony and requested that the judgment be reformed to accurately reflect the offense name and applicable statute. The appellate court agreed with Bush’s request for reformation, acknowledging the State’s concurrence that the judgment mistakenly identified the offense and cited the wrong statutory provision.

The case involved allegations against Bush for continuous sexual abuse of a child under fourteen, with the jury ultimately convicting him of the lesser-included offense of indecency with a child by contact. Expert testimony presented by the State explored the dynamics of child abuse, including general characteristics of perpetrators and the impact of a child’s outcry on siblings. Bush’s appeal challenged the relevance and prejudicial nature of this testimony, arguing it was speculative and did not directly pertain to the specifics of his case.

The appellate court found that any error in admitting the expert testimony was harmless, considering the substantial evidence of Bush’s guilt, including detailed testimonies from the complainants. The judgment was modified to correctly state Bush was convicted of indecency with a child by contact under Texas Penal Code section 21.11, affirming the trial court’s judgment as modified. This case underscores the appellate court’s role in ensuring trial court judgments accurately reflect the jury’s verdict and applicable laws.

What does an Indecency With a Child charge really mean?

The Texas Penal Code defines the charge of Indecency With a Child as follows:

(a) A person commits an offense if, with a child younger than 17 years of age, whether the child is of the same or opposite sex and regardless of whether the person knows the age of the child at the time of the offense, the person:

(1) engages in sexual contact with the child or causes the child to engage in sexual contact; or

(2) with intent to arouse or gratify the sexual desire of any person:

(A) exposes the person‘s anus or any part of the person‘s genitals, knowing the child is present; or

(B) causes the child to expose the child’s anus or any part of the child’s genitals.

Indecency with a Child by Contact

This version of the offense occurs when an individual engages in sexual contact with a child under the age of 17 who is not their spouse. “Sexual contact” is defined as the touching, including through clothing, of the anus, breast, or any part of the genitals of a child, carried out with the intent to arouse or gratify the sexual desire of any person.

This offense does not require penetration of any bodily orifices; such an act would typically escalate the charge to sexual assault. The behavior in question is often described as “fondling.” While it may seem less severe than explicit sexual acts, it can still lead to serious criminal charges upon conviction.

Indecency with a Child by Exposure

Indecency with a child by exposure happens when an individual exposes their anus or genitals in the presence of a child, knowing the child is there, or induces the child to expose their own anus or genitals, with the intention of sexually arousing or gratifying any person’s sexual desires.

Can I avoid sex offender registration if I’m facing Indecency with a Child charges?

Whether you are convicted or placed on deferred adjudication probation for Indecency with a Child, you will be required to register as a sex offender if you plead guilty. However, under Texas law, the amount of time that you will be required to register depends on several different factors. Additionally, it may be possible to negotiate for a reduction of the charge to something that is non-registerable.

Peace officers with the Texas Department of Public Safety, constable offices, and municipal police departments can make arrests for violations of Indecency With a Child in Dallas. Law enforcement agencies in Dallas that most typically make Indecency With a Child arrests include:

However, our trial preparation often commences well before the case is filed. From the onset of police investigation or arrest, we begin our proactive approach. While the state marshals its law enforcement resources to gather evidence, we counteract by meticulously scrutinizing and challenging their findings. As our client, you gain access to the comprehensive investigative capabilities of our entire legal team. With a cadre of dedicated professionals including paralegals, investigators, and forensic experts, we leverage our collective expertise to lay the groundwork for a robust defense strategy.

Attorney’s fees will vary. However, you can expect to pay from $15,000 to $40,000 on average for Indecency With a Child cases in Dallas. Some Dallas Indecency With a Child lawyers may charge much more depending on the complexity of the Dallas case. But be wary of lawyers who charge surprisingly low fees.

When consulting with a lawyer, remember to ask whether any any hourly fees apply. Additionally, most lawyers charge extra fees for trial, travel and expenses.

Even if someone has falsely accused you of Indecency With a Child, you should nevertheless still always take this charge very seriously. You may think that the state may “drop charges” against you because you are innocent. But absent effective advocacy by a lawyer, the state will often take the case to trial and let the jury decide.

If the state has charged you with Indecency With a Child, or if you are under investigation for the offense, then you should book an appointment or call us as soon as possible to speak with one of our Dallas Indecency With a Child attorneys.

How can you modify your Dallas bond conditions after an Indecency With a Child arrest?

Texas judges have broad power to set bail and bond conditions. However, sometimes judges impose overly harsh bond conditions and astronomically high bail. To get the best result, you should hire an attorney to help.

Practically speaking, if the police in Dallas have arrested you for Indecency With a Child, then the judge will typically impose a “no contact with the victim” bond condition. If you want to remove a no contact condition, then please book a consultation with us, and we will discuss what we can do for you.

What happens at a Dallas arraignment?

At your arraignment, a Dallas judge will hear your plea of not guilty. In Dallas, you may not have an attorney at your initial arraignment.
